set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 21
set1.q: A 38-year-old man has a foreign body sensation after a day of metalwork. Fluorescein shows several fine vertical lines running down the cornea. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Patch the eye and review in one week
The object needs to come out now.
Refer for urgent surgical exploration
It can be removed at the slit lamp.
Evert the upper eyelid
Correct. Vertical linear defects mean the object is under the upper lid, scraping with each blink.
Examine the lower fornix with a cotton bud
The vertical pattern points to the upper lid.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 36
set1.q: Which symptom indicates the macula has become involved in a retinal detachment?
opts: The eye has become painful
Detachment is characteristically painless.
Central visual acuity has dropped
Correct. Field defects come first; central acuity falls with macular involvement.
Floaters have increased
Floaters relate to the vitreous, not the macula.
Flashes have become more frequent
Flashes reflect traction rather than macular involvement.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 16
set1.q: A 36-year-old has a corneal laceration with a cut lens capsule and an opaque, swollen lens. When is lensectomy usually performed?
opts: At the same time as the globe repair, always
It is often deferred rather than done at once.
Only if vision fails to improve after a year
That is far later than described.
Never, since the lens will clear on its own
A hydrated opaque lens does not clear.
Later, once hyphema and inflammation settle
Correct. It is required but often deferred from the globe repair.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 21
set1.q: A 34-year-old machinist has photophobia, tearing and a foreign body sensation after a day at the lathe. Diffuse light shows nothing. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure and review in one week
The symptoms are unexplained.
Patch the eye and discharge
The cause has not been found.
Prescribe topical anaesthetic for comfort
Never prescribed for home use.
Slit lamp examination
Correct. Larger objects show on diffuse light; smaller ones need the slit lamp.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 27
set1.q: A 48-year-old has a deep laceration in the medial third of the lower lid. What is the consequence if it is not repaired properly?
opts: Chronic tearing
Correct. The canalicular injury is what makes the medial third special.
Permanent ptosis
That follows levator involvement, which is a different site.
Loss of central vision
The lid does not carry vision.
Corneal ulceration within days
Not the described consequence.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set1.q: A cycloplegic drop is prescribed for a patient with a hyphema. What is it doing?
opts: Lowering the intraocular pressure directly
That is the role of other agents.
Dissolving the clot
Nothing in the regimen dissolves it; aminocaproic acid slows breakdown.
Constricting the pupil to trap the blood
It does the opposite to the pupil.
Paralysing the ciliary body
Correct. Atropine, homatropine and scopolamine are used this way.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 3
set1.q: A 52-year-old is brought in after a road traffic collision with an obviously injured left eye, confusion and shallow breathing. Which is the most appropriate first action?
opts: Order computed tomography of the orbits
Imaging follows resuscitation.
Assess airway, breathing and circulation
Correct. The eye is assessed after the patient is stabilised.
Measure visual acuity in both eyes
Acuity waits until the primary survey is done.
Instil fluorescein and examine the cornea
The surface examination is not the first action.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 36
set1.q: A 55-year-old with a fresh retinal detachment asks how urgently she needs to be seen. Which is the most accurate response?
opts: Only if the curtain spreads further
Referral does not wait on progression.
Immediately, but only if the other eye is affected too
One eye is enough.
By an ophthalmologist within 24 hours
Correct. The referral is immediate.
At the next available clinic within a month
Far too slow.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 35
set1.q: A 59-year-old describes flashes for two weeks, then a curtain yesterday. Which sequence explains this?
opts: Retinal break first, then vitreous liquefaction
The vitreous change usually comes first.
Choroidal neovascularisation with haemorrhage
That is macular degeneration.
Optic nerve inflammation
That gives painful loss with colour desaturation.
Vitreous detachment, then a retinal break
Correct. That is the usual order of events.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17
set1.q: A 34-year-old man was struck in the right eye by a baseball. The lid is swollen, the conjunctiva is deeply haemorrhagic and the globe feels soft. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Shield the eye and call ophthalmology
Correct. A soft eye with massive haemorrhagic chemosis after blunt force is a globe rupture until proven otherwise.
Measure the intraocular pressure
Pressing on a possibly open globe risks extruding its contents.
Instil a mydriatic and examine the fundus
The eye is never dilated when trauma is suspected.
Irrigate the eye with copious saline
Irrigation does nothing for a ruptured globe and adds pressure.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 24
set1.q: A 28-year-old has a hyphema and a distorted pupil after a penetrating injury. Which step must be omitted?
opts: Calling ophthalmology
That is part of management.
Measuring the pressure
Correct. Pressing on a possibly open globe risks extruding its contents.
Placing a rigid shield
That is exactly what should be done.
Giving an antiemetic
That is part of management.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 33
set1.q: A 68-year-old on apixaban develops painful proptosis of one eye over an hour with no injury. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
That does not cause proptosis.
Periorbital haematoma
Correct. It is not always traumatic, and anticoagulants are a listed cause.
Orbital cellulitis
That is infective, usually with fever and a longer course.
Thyroid eye disease
That develops over months and is usually bilateral.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43
set1.q: A patient's optic nerve was damaged at the moment of an orbital injury. What should be expected from surgery?
opts: Surgery reliably restores the lost vision
It does not.
Surgery restores vision if done within 24 hours
Timing does not change this.
Vision recovers spontaneously in most cases
Not what is described.
It is unlikely to improve, and surgery may worsen it
Correct. That is why the decision is made carefully.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set1.q: A 26-year-old was punched in the eye. He has periorbital swelling, numbness of the cheek, and double vision when looking upward. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Blowout fracture with inferior rectus entrapment
Correct. Infraorbital numbness with upward gaze diplopia is the combination.
Third nerve palsy
That gives ptosis and a dilated pupil.
Traumatic optic neuropathy
That reduces vision rather than restricting upgaze.
Orbital cellulitis
That is infective, with fever and proptosis.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 22
set1.q: A conjunctival foreign body is visible on diffuse light examination in a 28-year-old. Which is the most appropriate removal method?
opts: Referral for operative removal
That is disproportionate for a conjunctival object.
A cotton-tipped applicator
Correct. A conjunctival object lifts off with a swab.
A sterile 27-gauge needle
That is for a corneal foreign body.
A battery-operated burr
That is for a rust ring.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17
set1.q: A 55-year-old has a confirmed globe rupture. Which is the definitive management?
opts: Topical antibiotics and observation
That does not close an open globe.
Intravitreal antibiotics alone
That does not repair the wound.
Immediate surgical repair
Correct. Everything else is holding measures until then.
Pressure patching and review in 24 hours
Pressure is exactly what to avoid.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 14
set1.q: A 47-year-old struck by a metal shard has an eye in which the pupil is drawn to one side toward a corneal wound and the anterior chamber looks flat. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Open globe injury
Correct. A pupil pulled toward the wound with a flat chamber is the picture.
Corneal abrasion
An abrasion does not distort the pupil.
Anterior uveitis
Inflammation may constrict the pupil but does not flatten the chamber.
Acute angle closure
That gives a mid-dilated fixed pupil and a hazy cornea.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 9
set1.q: A conscious and cooperative 33-year-old has a periorbital laceration after an assault. Which examination elements are appropriate?
opts: Gonioscopy of the drainage angle
Not part of the trauma assessment.
Corneal sensation testing alone
Too narrow an examination.
Inspection, pupils, acuity and fields
Correct, done without causing further damage.
Dilated fundoscopy first
The eye is not dilated when trauma is suspected.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44
set1.q: A 44-year-old has clear rhinorrhoea after a fall. Which two bedside findings would support cerebrospinal fluid rather than nasal secretions?
opts: A positive dextrose stick and a halo sign
Correct. Those are the two bedside tests described.
A negative dextrose stick and clear fluid
A negative stick argues against it.
Purulent colour and a foul smell
That suggests infection instead.
Fluorescein uptake and photophobia
Those relate to the cornea.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set1.q: A 30-year-old with a hyphema asks how long the dangerous period lasts. Which is the most accurate response?
opts: The first 24 hours only
The window is longer than a day.
There is no dangerous period once bleeding stops
Rebleeding is the whole concern.
The first month, evenly throughout
The risk is concentrated much earlier.
The first 72 hours, when most rebleeding happens
Correct. A secondary haemorrhage is what costs vision permanently.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set1.q: A 15-year-old with sickle cell disease sustains a hyphema. Why does that history matter?
opts: It makes aminocaproic acid unnecessary
It does not remove the need to prevent a rebleed.
It means the pressure need not be checked
Pressure is still measured unless the globe may be open.
It raises the risk of complications
Correct. Sickle cell disease is specifically flagged.
It rules out a rebleed
It does the opposite.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44
set1.q: Which combination of findings should raise a basilar skull fracture after head trauma?
opts: Raccoon eyes, Battle sign and haemotympanum
Correct. Those are the indirect signs.
Ptosis, a dilated pupil and diplopia
That points to a third nerve palsy.
A red eye with discharge and lid crusting
That is an infective surface picture.
Diplopia on upward gaze with cheek numbness
That points to an orbital floor fracture.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43
set1.q: A 32-year-old has an orbital floor fracture with no entrapment, no globe injury and a clear maxillary sinus. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Antibiotics and admission
Antibiotics follow blood in the maxillary sinus.
Neurosurgical consult
That is the basilar skull fracture pathway.
Immediate ophthalmology consult for a true blowout
That applies to a true blowout, which this is being managed as without.
Ice and analgesia, with follow-up in 2 to 3 days
Correct. That is the pathway when nothing else is involved.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43
set1.q: A 44-year-old has an orbital floor fracture with no entrapment and no globe injury, and blood is seen in the maxillary sinus. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Neurosurgical admission
Not indicated for this fracture.
Ice, analgesia and antibiotics
Correct. Blood in the sinus is what adds the antibiotic.
Immediate operative repair
Not required without entrapment or globe injury.
Ice and analgesia alone
Blood in the sinus adds an antibiotic.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set1.q: A 29-year-old has a wooden splinter driven into the periorbital tissue while gardening. Beyond removing nothing and imaging appropriately, which additional step is required?
opts: Confirm tetanus is up to date
Correct. Penetration with metal or organic material carries the risk.
Start systemic antivirals
There is no viral indication here.
Give a mydriatic to examine the retina
The eye is not dilated in trauma.
Begin oral corticosteroids
Not indicated for a penetrating splinter.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 47
set1.q: A patient with a suspected basilar skull fracture has clear fluid dripping from the nose that forms a double ring on the pillowcase. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Neurosurgery consult and admission
Correct. A cerebrospinal fluid leak forces both.
Nasal packing to stop the drainage
Packing a cerebrospinal fluid leak is not the answer.
Ophthalmology consult
The relevant specialty is neurosurgery.
Prophylactic antibiotics alone, then discharge
Antibiotics here are themselves debated, and do not replace admission.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 27
set1.q: A 50-year-old has a laceration involving the tarsal plate of the upper lid. Which is the most appropriate action?
opts: Leave it open for 24 hours then close it
That practice is for facial lacerations, not the tarsal plate.
Refer routinely in 2 to 3 weeks
Too slow for this criterion.
Consult ophthalmology
Correct. Tarsal plate involvement is an explicit referral criterion.
Repair it with absorbable sutures in the department
Tarsal plate involvement takes it out of department repair.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44
set1.q: A 39-year-old fell from a ladder. She has bruising around both eyes, bruising behind one ear, and blood behind the eardrum. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Periorbital cellulitis
That is infective and unilateral.
Basilar skull fracture
Correct. Raccoon eyes, Battle sign and haemotympanum together.
Bilateral orbital floor fractures
Those do not produce Battle sign or haemotympanum.
Nasal fracture with periorbital spread
That does not explain the retroauricular bruising.

set1.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for common ophthalmological disorders by age
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 18
set1.q: A 12-year-old scratched his cornea playing. His parent asks for anaesthetic drops for the pain at home. Which is the most appropriate response?
opts: Prescribe a corticosteroid drop instead
Steroids are not the treatment for an abrasion.
Prescribe nothing at all
An antibiotic and analgesia are still appropriate.
Decline, because they delay healing and can cause an ulcer
Correct. This holds at any age.
Prescribe them for 24 hours only
A shorter course carries the same risks.

set1.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set1.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 18
set1.q: A 27-year-old woman scratched her cornea removing a contact lens. Fluorescein confirms an abrasion. She asks for something for the pain to use at home. Which is the most appropriate response?
opts: No treatment, since abrasions heal regardless
An antibiotic and review are part of care.
Analgesia and a topical antibiotic
Correct. Take-home anaesthetic delays healing, masks worsening symptoms and can cause a corneal ulcer.
Topical anaesthetic drops four times daily
That is the one thing that must not be sent home.
Topical corticosteroid drops for comfort
Steroids are not the treatment for an abrasion.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 18
set2.q: A 42-year-old treated for a corneal abrasion three days ago returns with worsening pain and a white spot on the cornea. Which is the most likely explanation?
opts: A rust ring has formed spontaneously
Rust rings follow metallic foreign bodies, not abrasions.
A hyphema has developed
That is blood in the chamber, not a corneal white spot.
A corneal ulcer has developed
Correct. This is why abrasions are re-examined, and why anaesthetic drops are never sent home.
The abrasion is healing normally
Worsening pain with an infiltrate is not normal healing.

set2.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for common ophthalmological disorders by age
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set2.q: An 8-year-old struck by a ball has severe pain, vomiting and a heart rate of 48 whenever he tries to look up. His eye and lids look normal. Which is the most likely explanation?
opts: Migraine triggered by the injury
That does not restrict upgaze with autonomic signs.
A white-eyed blowout
Correct. In children entrapment can occur with no orbital soft tissue signs at all.
Simple concussion
Concussion does not produce gaze-provoked bradycardia.
Vasovagal syncope from pain
The symptoms are provoked specifically by eye movement.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 31
set2.q: Why does the bruising in an orbital contusion stay in front of the eye rather than spreading behind it?
opts: The periosteum is impermeable
Not the described mechanism.
Venous drainage carries it forward
Not the described mechanism.
The septum acts as a wall
Correct. That is what keeps it preseptal.
The orbital fat absorbs the blood
Not the described mechanism.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set2.q: A 19-year-old arrives with a fish hook embedded through the cornea. He is stable and in pain. Which is the most appropriate management of the hook?
opts: Leave it in place and arrange surgical repair
Correct. It may be tamponading the wound, and removing it can extrude intraocular contents.
Withdraw it along its entry path
Withdrawal risks extrusion of intraocular contents.
Cut it flush with the cornea and cover it
Manipulation carries the same risk.
Remove it after topical anaesthetic
Anaesthesia does not make removal safe.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set2.q: A 41-year-old welder felt something strike his eye while grinding without goggles. Vision is 20/40 and the eye is quiet. Which imaging is appropriate, and which must be avoided?
opts: Computed tomography of the orbit; avoid magnetic resonance imaging
Correct. A magnetic field can move a metallic fragment through the eye.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit; avoid computed tomography
That reverses the safe choice.
Ocular ultrasound with firm probe pressure; avoid computed tomography
Probe pressure is unsafe if the globe may be open.
No imaging, since acuity is preserved
Vision can be normal with a retained intraocular fragment.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 39
set2.q: A 64-year-old with long-standing proliferative diabetic retinopathy has a localised, concave retinal detachment. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Treat the underlying systemic disease alone
That is the approach for an exudative detachment.
Observation with serial imaging
Not the described management.
Intravitreal antibiotics
There is no infection.
Surgical repair
Correct. A traction detachment is managed surgically.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set2.q: A 26-year-old with hyphema has an intraocular pressure of 34 mmHg (normal 10 to 21) and no suspicion of an open globe. Which agents are used?
opts: Topical corticosteroids alone
Steroids are part of care but do not lower pressure.
Aspirin to improve perfusion
Aspirin raises the rebleed risk and is avoided.
A mydriatic to open the angle
Dilation is not used in ocular trauma.
Beta blockers and acetazolamide
Correct. That is how a raised pressure is brought down here.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set2.q: A 37-year-old has crepitus in the eyelid after blowing his nose following facial trauma. Which finding is this?
opts: Subcutaneous emphysema
Correct. Air tracks from the sinus into the orbit through the fracture.
Orbital cellulitis
That is infective, with fever and proptosis.
Chemosis
That is conjunctival oedema.
Enophthalmos
That is the eye sitting back, not air in the tissue.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43
set2.q: A 40-year-old is suspected of an orbital fracture after a blow. Which imaging is ordered?
opts: Plain facial radiographs alone
They do not adequately define the fracture.
Ocular ultrasound
It does not assess bone.
No imaging unless diplopia is present
Imaging is not withheld on that basis.
Computed tomography of the orbits and midface
Correct. That is the study for this fracture.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 31
set2.q: A 35-year-old has periorbital swelling and ecchymosis after a fall, with a normal globe and no haemorrhage within the orbit. Beyond supportive care, which is the most appropriate step?
opts: Start topical antibiotics
There is no surface infection.
Arrange urgent canthotomy
There is no orbital haemorrhage to decompress.
Refer for cataract assessment
Not relevant acutely.
Exclude brain trauma
Correct. The force that bruised the orbit reaches the brain.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 8
set2.q: A 25-year-old with an eye injury is intoxicated and gives an inconsistent account. Which is the most appropriate way to establish the mechanism?
opts: Accept the account as given
An inconsistent account leaves the mechanism unknown.
Record the mechanism as unknown and proceed
A collateral history is available and useful.
Ask family, friends or bystanders
Correct. The circumstance of injury still has to be established.
Wait until he is sober to take a history
Delay costs time in an injury that may need surgery.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set2.q: A 22-year-old with a traumatic hyphema is admitted. Which regimen fits, and what is it aiming at?
opts: Topical anaesthetic and discharge, with review in a week
This needs monitoring, not discharge.
Bed rest head-up and aminocaproic acid, to prevent a rebleed
Correct. Every element serves that one goal.
Ambulation and warm compresses, to clear the blood faster
Speed of clearance is not the aim, and activity risks a rebleed.
Aspirin, to prevent clot organisation
Aspirin raises the risk of a secondary haemorrhage.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 24
set2.q: A 16-year-old was hit in the eye by a paintball. There is a layer of blood across the lower anterior chamber with a visible fluid level. Which is the most likely diagnosis, and what else must be considered?
opts: Traumatic iritis with cells in the chamber
Cells are not a layered blood level.
Hyphema, and it can itself indicate an open globe
Correct. It is not always an isolated injury.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage overlying the iris
That sits on the surface, outside the chamber.
Vitreous haemorrhage seen through the pupil
That lies behind the lens.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 22
set2.q: A metallic corneal foreign body is removed from a 45-year-old, leaving a brown ring in the stroma. Which is the most appropriate management of that ring?
opts: Wipe it with a cotton-tipped applicator
That is for conjunctival foreign bodies.
Leave it, since it will resorb
It does not resorb on its own.
Remove it with a battery-operated burr
Correct. A rust ring from iron or copper comes out with a burr.
Irrigate repeatedly with saline
Irrigation will not lift a rust ring.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 41
set2.q: A 29-year-old has double vision on looking to the side after blunt orbital trauma. Which muscle is entrapped?
opts: Inferior oblique
Not the muscle described.
Medial rectus
Correct. Lateral gaze diplopia points to the medial rectus and a medial wall fracture.
Inferior rectus
That gives diplopia on upward gaze.
Superior rectus
Not the muscle entrapped in these fractures.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 39
set2.q: A 61-year-old with hypertension and a known intraocular tumour has subretinal fluid but no retinal break on dilated examination. Which type of detachment is this?
opts: Posterior vitreous detachment
That is a separate event, not a retinal detachment.
Exudative
Correct. No break and no traction, with an associated tumour.
Traction
That requires fibrovascular traction, usually diabetic.
Combined rhegmatogenous and traction
Neither element is present.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 26
set2.q: A 21-year-old has a full-thickness upper lid laceration. Beyond repairing the lid, which is the most important step?
opts: Patch the eye for 48 hours
That does not address the globe.
Prescribe a cycloplegic
Not the priority here.
Examine the globe underneath
Correct. About two thirds of full-thickness lid lacerations come with one.
Start oral corticosteroids
Not indicated.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set2.q: A 23-year-old has a laceration of the upper lid and a subconjunctival haemorrhage after being struck with a bottle. He is alert. Which is the most appropriate next step before any lid repair?
opts: Measure the intraocular pressure first
Unsafe if the globe may be open.
Assess the globe beneath
Correct. Two thirds of full-thickness lid lacerations have a globe injury with them.
Close the lid and arrange follow-up
Closing over an unrecognised open globe is the error to avoid.
Instil a mydriatic to see the retina
The eye is not dilated in trauma.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 44
set2.q: Which bones may be involved in a basilar skull fracture?
opts: The nasal bones and the vomer
Those are not the skull base.
The parietal bones only
The parietal bone is not the base.
Ethmoid, frontal, temporal, sphenoid or occipital
Correct. Those make up the skull base.
The maxilla and the zygomatic arch alone
Those are facial bones, not the skull base.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 36
set2.q: A 58-year-old myope describes a shower of floaters, flashes of light, and a curtain moving across the vision of one eye. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Central retinal vein occlusion
That gives sudden painless loss without flashes.
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Correct. Flashes, floaters and a curtain, with myopia as the risk factor.
Exudative retinal detachment
That has no break and usually accompanies systemic disease or a tumour.
Traction retinal detachment
That follows proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 39
set2.q: A 52-year-old has subretinal fluid with no retinal break and no traction, alongside a known intraocular tumour. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Treat the underlying condition
Correct. An exudative detachment is not primarily surgical.
Scleral buckling
Surgery is not the primary answer here.
Pneumatic retinopexy
Not indicated without a break.
Observation with no treatment
The underlying disease is treated.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 43
set2.q: Computed tomography confirms an orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment in a 30-year-old. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Contact a facial trauma surgeon urgently
Correct. An entrapped muscle can necrose if its blood supply is compromised.
Ice, analgesia and review in 2 to 3 days
That is the pathway when there is no entrapment.
Admit for neurosurgical observation
That is the basilar skull fracture pathway.
Start antibiotics and discharge
Antibiotics are for blood in the maxillary sinus.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 18
set2.q: A 31-year-old has a corneal abrasion from a fingernail. Which treatment is appropriate?
opts: A topical corticosteroid
Steroids are not the treatment for an abrasion.
No treatment and no follow-up
Antibiotic cover and re-examination are both part of care.
A topical antibacterial
Correct, and patching may ease the pain.
A topical antiviral
There is no viral indication.

set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 26
set2.q: A 33-year-old has a 1 centimetre laceration running through the lower lid margin after a dog bite. Which is the most appropriate disposition?
opts: Close it in the emergency department with fine sutures
Margin involvement takes it out of emergency department repair.
Leave it open and review in one week
A margin laceration needs proper repair.
Refer to plastic surgery as an outpatient
Ophthalmology is the named specialty.
Ophthalmology, because the lid margin is involved
Correct. Margin involvement is one of the explicit referral criteria.

set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17
set2.q: A 72-year-old with previous cataract surgery in both eyes is struck in the face by a car airbag. Why does the surgical history matter here?
opts: Old incisions leave a permanent weak point
Correct. Prior intraocular surgery lowers the force needed.
It makes a hyphema more likely than a rupture
Not the reason the history matters.
It protects the eye from blunt force
It does the opposite.
It rules out an open globe
It raises the concern rather than excluding it.

set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 6
set2.q: A 45-year-old on warfarin fell and struck his face, and is now confused. His right eye is bruised. Which is the most appropriate imaging decision?
opts: No imaging unless vision is reduced
Confusion and anticoagulation are themselves the indication.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the head
Computed tomography is the study described.
Plain skull radiographs
They do not answer the question.
Computed tomography without contrast
Correct. Both are on the list that makes imaging automatic.

set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 8
set2.q: Which detail about the mechanism most changes the level of concern in ocular trauma?
opts: Blunt or sharp, high or low velocity
Correct. That is what predicts the injury pattern.
Whether the patient was wearing spectacles
Useful but not the key mechanism detail.
The time of day the injury happened
Not what changes concern.
The patient's occupation alone
Occupation hints at exposure but the mechanism is what matters.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 26
set2.q: Which of these lid lacerations can reasonably be repaired in the emergency department?
opts: A superficial skin cut sparing the margin
Correct. Partial-thickness lacerations meeting none of the criteria are repaired there.
A cut 4 millimetres from the medial canthus
Within 6 to 8 millimetres of the canthus is a referral criterion.
A cut associated with new ptosis
Ptosis is a referral criterion.
A cut through the tarsal plate
Tarsal plate involvement is a referral criterion.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 33
set2.q: A 60-year-old on warfarin develops a tense, proptotic orbit with rising pressure and no history of injury. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Pressure patching the eye
Pressure is the wrong direction entirely.
Topical beta blocker alone
It will not decompress the orbit.
Immediate enucleation
Far beyond what is required.
Canthotomy with cantholysis
Correct. Releasing the lateral canthal tendon and cutting its inferior branch lets the blood drain.

set2.io: a — Ocular trauma: etiology, manifestations, testing, management, referral, prognosis
set2.cite: CMS I Ocular Trauma - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 25
set2.q: A 20-year-old with a hyphema is being discharged after admission. Which instruction matters most?
opts: Stop the cycloplegic once the pain settles
The regimen is not stopped on symptoms alone.
Avoid aspirin, antiplatelets and straining
Correct. Both raise the risk of a secondary haemorrhage.
Use topical anaesthetic drops when the eye aches
Never prescribed for home use.
Resume contact sport as soon as the blood clears
That invites another injury.
